overview:
Jinasena (c. 8th–9th century CE) is one of the most influential acharyas of the Digambara Jain tradition and a central figure in the development of Jain Sanskrit puranic literature. Active in the Deccan under the Rashtrakuta dynasty, he is best known as the author of the Ādipurāṇa and as the principal architect of the Mahāpurāṇa, a vast universal history that integrates narratives of the Tirthankaras, Jain cosmology, and ethical reflection. He served as the spiritual preceptor (rājaguru) to the Rashtrakuta emperor Amoghavarṣa I, which placed him at the intersection of royal power, religious authority, and literary production.

Historically, Jinasena is situated within the lineage of Digambara scholasticism that centers on the canonical text Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama. His guru was the eminent acharya Virasena, under whom he received rigorous training in doctrine and scriptural exegesis. After Virasena’s death, Jinasena completed the Dhāvalā commentary on Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama, thereby helping to secure the text’s status as a foundational authority in the Digambara canon. This work marks him not only as a puranic storyteller but also as a technical exegete deeply engaged with karma theory, cosmology, and the structure of the path to liberation.

The Ādipurāṇa, Jinasena’s most celebrated independent composition, narrates the life of the first Tirthankara Ṛṣabhanātha (Ādinātha) and his sons, especially the monk Bāhubali. It presents the Jain version of primordial human history: the emergence of social organization, arts, and technologies under Ṛṣabha’s guidance, and the paradigmatic renunciation of worldly power in favor of asceticism. Through ornate Sanskrit verse, Jinasena weaves together hagiography, didactic reflection, and cosmological motifs, offering a model of Jain kingship and lay conduct that is grounded in non-violence, restraint, and charity (dāna).

The Mahāpurāṇa, conceived by Jinasena and completed by his disciple Guṇabhadra, extends this narrative frame to encompass the lives of multiple Tirthankaras and a broader universal history. It is often divided into Ādipurāṇa (Jinasena’s portion) and Uttarapurāṇa (primarily Guṇabhadra’s continuation). Within this work, Jinasena articulates a strong critique of the idea of a creator-god, emphasizing instead the Jain doctrine of an eternal, beginningless universe governed by the laws of karma and the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of substances. His arguments against creationism are framed philosophically rather than polemically, and they serve to clarify the Jain view that liberation arises from self-effort and right knowledge, not divine intervention.

Beyond his literary achievements, Jinasena’s role as rājaguru to Amoghavarṣa I had lasting implications for the religious landscape of the Deccan. Epigraphic and literary traditions portray the king as deeply devoted to Jainism, and Jinasena is credited with shaping royal policy in ways that favored Jain institutions and ethics. He is also associated with prescriptive teachings on ritual purity and social conduct, including restrictions on the use of meat and honey in Jain rituals due to their connection with violence, and nuanced positions on the wearing of sacred threads and garments by different social groups. These teachings reflect an attempt to harmonize Jain non-violence with the social realities of caste and profession, while maintaining a distinct Jain identity.

The name “Jinasena” actually refers to at least two historically distinct Digambara acharyas. The later Jinasena, discussed above, is the author of Ādipurāṇa and the initiator of Mahāpurāṇa, active in the 8th–9th centuries and linked to the Rashtrakuta court. An earlier Jinasena, associated with the Punnāṭa Saṅgha, composed the Harivaṃśapurāṇa, a Jain retelling of the Kṛṣṇa narrative that parallels and reinterprets themes from the Mahābhārata. Modern scholarship and traditional catalogues carefully distinguish these figures by sectarian affiliation, textual corpus, and chronological context, but popular references sometimes conflate them. Any careful study of “Jinasena” must therefore specify which acharya and which text tradition is in view.

In Jain intellectual history, Jinasena stands at a crossroads: he inherits the technical doctrinal legacy of Virasena and the Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama tradition, while also pioneering a sophisticated puranic literature in polished Sanskrit that could speak both to Jain communities and to broader royal and scholarly audiences. His works continue to be edited, translated, and studied in modern Jain scholarship, and they remain central sources for understanding Digambara views on cosmology, ethics, kingship, and the narrative imagination of Jainism.

primary_sources.title: Ādipurāṇa
primary_sources.author: Acharya Jinasena (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: Ādipurāṇa is Jinasena’s extensive Sanskrit poetic narrative of the first Tirthankara Ṛṣabhanātha (Ādinātha), his family, and the origins of human civilization. It recounts how Ṛṣabha teaches people agriculture, crafts, and social organization, and then renounces worldly life to become an ascetic, establishing the paradigm of Jain renunciation. The text also narrates the story of Bāhubali, whose victory in battle is followed by a profound renunciation, illustrating the Jain ideal that true conquest is self-conquest rather than domination of others.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B: primary text in verified editions, often studied with traditional commentaries. Modern critical editions and translations (e.g., in the Murtidevi Jaina Granthamala series) provide Sanskrit text with Hindi or English translation. The work is central to Digambara narrative theology and is a key source for Jain accounts of Ṛṣabhanātha and Bāhubali.

primary_sources.title: Mahāpurāṇa (including Ādipurāṇa and Uttarapurāṇa)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Jinasena (Ādipurāṇa portion) and Acharya Guṇabhadra (Uttarapurāṇa portion)
primary_sources.translation: Mahāpurāṇa is an encyclopedic Jain universal history that integrates the lives of multiple Tirthankaras, cosmological cycles, and ethical teachings. Jinasena’s Ādipurāṇa portion lays the foundation with the narrative of Ṛṣabhanātha and early human history, while Guṇabhadra’s Uttarapurāṇa continues with subsequent Tirthankaras and legendary figures. Within this work, Jinasena articulates a philosophical critique of the doctrine of a creator-god, emphasizing that the universe is beginningless and governed by karma and the intrinsic nature of substances, and that liberation is achieved through self-discipline and right knowledge.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B: primary text with traditional commentaries. Frequently cited in discussions of Jain cosmology and the Jain critique of creationism. The famous anti-creationist passage often quoted in modern literature and popularized by figures like Carl Sagan is drawn from this text, though translations and paraphrases vary and should be checked against critical editions.

primary_sources.title: Dhāvalā (commentary on Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama)
primary_sources.author: Acharya Virasena (principal author), completed by Acharya Jinasena
primary_sources.translation: Dhāvalā is a monumental Sanskrit and Prakrit commentary on the Digambara canonical text Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama, which analyzes the structure of karma, the categories of reality, and the stages of spiritual development. Virasena initiated the commentary, and after his death, Jinasena completed significant portions, thereby ensuring the transmission and systematization of complex doctrinal material. The work is highly technical, focusing on the classification of karmic particles, their bondage, fruition, and the progression through the guṇasthānas (spiritual stages).
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B: canonical text and major traditional commentary. Dhāvalā is central to the Digambara scholastic tradition and is a primary source for detailed karma theory and doctrinal analysis. Jinasena’s role as completer of the commentary links him directly to the heart of Digambara scriptural exegesis, beyond his more widely known puranic compositions.

primary_sources.title: Harivaṃśapurāṇa
primary_sources.author: Earlier Acharya Jinasena of the Punnāṭa Saṅgha (Digambara)
primary_sources.translation: Harivaṃśapurāṇa is a Jain puranic retelling of the life of Kṛṣṇa and related figures, paralleling and reinterpreting themes from the Hindu Mahābhārata and Harivaṃśa traditions. It presents Kṛṣṇa within a Jain ethical and cosmological framework, emphasizing non-violence, restraint, and the karmic consequences of actions. The text is structured as a narrative purāṇa, using familiar epic motifs to convey distinctly Jain doctrinal and moral teachings.
primary_sources.notes: Corpus tier A/B: primary text in verified editions. Although attributed to an acharya named Jinasena, this is a different historical figure from the later Jinasena associated with Ādipurāṇa and Mahāpurāṇa. Modern scholarship and traditional catalogues distinguish the two by sectarian lineage (e.g., Punnāṭa Saṅgha vs. Panchāstūpanvaya), chronology, and textual corpus. Confusion between these two Jinasenas is a common issue in secondary literature and popular references.

misconceptions.myth: There was only one Acharya Jinasena, and he wrote all the major Jain puranas including Ādipurāṇa, Mahāpurāṇa, and Harivaṃśapurāṇa.
misconceptions.reality: The name “Jinasena” refers to at least two distinct Digambara acharyas. The later Jinasena (8th–9th century CE), disciple of Virasena and rājaguru to Amoghavarṣa I, is the author of Ādipurāṇa and the initiator of Mahāpurāṇa, and he completed the Dhāvalā commentary on Ṣaṭkhaṅḍāgama. An earlier Jinasena, associated with the Punnāṭa Saṅgha, composed Harivaṃśapurāṇa. Careful study must distinguish these figures by lineage, chronology, and textual corpus.

misconceptions.myth: Jinasena’s critique of a creator-god in Mahāpurāṇa means that Jainism is simply atheistic and rejects all forms of divinity.
misconceptions.reality: Jinasena’s arguments in Mahāpurāṇa reject the idea of a single creator-god who makes, sustains, and destroys the universe. This is consistent with Jain doctrine, which holds that the universe is beginningless and governed by karma and the intrinsic nature of substances. However, Jainism affirms the existence of liberated beings (siddhas) and perfected teachers (Tirthankaras) as objects of reverence, even though they do not create or control the universe. Jinasena’s critique is directed at creationism, not at the broader Jain concept of spiritual perfection and worthy veneration.

misconceptions.myth: Because Jinasena emphasized non-violence and purity, he completely rejected all ritual and social norms, advocating a purely ascetic, anti-social ideal.
misconceptions.reality: Jinasena strongly emphasized non-violence, including prohibitions on using meat, honey, and similar materials in Jain rituals due to their connection with harm. At the same time, his teachings and narrative works recognize the realities of social life, including distinctions of profession and status. He allowed certain garments for artisans and other groups while restricting symbols like the sacred thread in specific contexts, and he highlighted the importance of charity (dāna) for householders. His vision integrates rigorous ethical restraint with a realistic engagement with lay life, rather than rejecting social norms altogether.

misconceptions.myth: Ādipurāṇa is only a devotional hagiography with no doctrinal or historical significance for Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: While Ādipurāṇa is richly devotional and hagiographic, it also serves as a key doctrinal and cultural text. It presents Jain models of kingship, renunciation, and lay conduct; narrates the origins of arts, crafts, and social organization under Ṛṣabhanātha; and embeds Jain cosmological and ethical themes in narrative form. For Digambara tradition, it is a major source for understanding the first Tirthankara, the figure of Bāhubali, and the Jain vision of primordial human history.
